chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
topic: The Big Questions: what moves prices
prompt: Mangoes are costly at the start of the season and much cheaper a few weeks later. According to the chapter, the prices of snacks, movie tickets, phones, vegetables and all other goods and services are decided by which **two powerful forces**?

image.alt: Two mango stalls, one early in the season and one later, with price tags

hint: One force comes from buyers, the other from sellers.
explanation: The chapter says prices do not change randomly: they are set by **demand** (what buyers want and can pay for) and **supply** (what sellers offer). Seasons, festivals, trends and even rumours matter only because they change demand or supply. Early in the season few mangoes reach the market, so they are dear; when the harvest arrives in bulk, the price falls.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: A bicycle costs ₹6,000. Which of these children is creating **demand** for it, in the economic sense?

image.alt: A bicycle with a price tag between two children

options.text: Anu, who wants it badly but has no money and no way to pay
Ravi, who looks at a poster of it and wishes he had one
Meera, who has ₹6,000 but has no interest in cycling
Kabir, who has saved ₹6,000 and is ready to buy it at that price

hint: Demand needs two things together: the wish to buy and something more.
explanation: **Demand** is the quantity people are **willing and able** to buy at a particular price. It is not just desire: the willingness must be backed by **purchasing power**, a measure of how much a unit of money can buy at a particular time. Anu and Ravi only wish for the cycle, and Meera can pay but is not willing, so only Kabir's wish counts as demand.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A price board for mangoes next to a shopping bag of mangoes

assertion: When the price of mangoes fell from ₹150 to ₹100 and then to ₹50 per kg, Srivalli bought 1 kg, then 2 kg, then 3 kg.
reason: The Law of Demand states that the price of a good and its quantity demanded move in the same direction.
hint: As the price went down, did the quantity go down too?
explanation: The assertion is true: it is the chapter's own example of Srivalli's **individual demand**. The reason is false. The **Law of Demand** describes an **inverse** relationship: when price falls, quantity demanded rises, and when price rises, quantity demanded falls (other things remaining the same). Price and quantity moving in the same direction describes the law of **supply**.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: Srivalli's demand schedule is: ₹150 → 1 kg, ₹100 → 2 kg, ₹50 → 3 kg. Tap the point that shows how many mangoes she buys when the price is **₹100 per kg**.

image.alt: A demand curve for mangoes with numbered markers

hint: Go across from ₹100 on the price axis until you meet the red line.
explanation: Price is on the **y-axis** and quantity on the **x-axis**. Going across from ₹100 meets the curve above 2 kg, so that point shows Srivalli buying **2 kg at ₹100**. Joining the three points gives the downward-sloping **demand curve DD’**. The two marked spots that are off the line pair a price with the wrong quantity.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: Using Srivalli's demand schedule (₹150 → 1 kg, ₹100 → 2 kg, ₹50 → 3 kg), at which price does she **spend the most money** on mangoes?

image.alt: A demand curve for mangoes with three plotted points

options.text: ₹50 per kg, because she buys the most
₹150 per kg, because the price is highest
She spends the same amount at every price

hint: Total spending = price × quantity. Work it out for each row.
explanation: Total spending = price × quantity: ₹150 × 1 = ₹150, ₹100 × 2 = **₹200**, and ₹50 × 3 = ₹150. So she spends the most at **₹100 per kg**. Buying the largest quantity (3 kg) or paying the highest price (₹150) does not by itself give the biggest bill, because the other factor is small. The three amounts are not equal, so the last option is wrong too.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: Arrange the steps for turning a demand schedule into a demand curve.

image.alt: A small price and quantity table with an arrow pointing to a graph

items.text: Mark one point for each price–quantity pair
Write down the quantity bought at each price in a table (the demand schedule)
Join the points to get a downward-sloping demand curve
Draw the axes: price on the y-axis and quantity on the x-axis

hint: You need the numbers before you can plot anything.
explanation: A **demand schedule** is a table of prices and the quantities demanded; drawn on a graph, it becomes the **demand curve**. In the chapter, Srivalli's points A (1 kg at ₹150), B (2 kg at ₹100) and C (3 kg at ₹50) are joined to give the **downward-sloping** curve DD’, which shows the inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded.

image.alt: A table of how many kilograms of guava four friends would buy at four prices

hint: Market demand is the sum of all the buyers' demands at the same price.
explanation: **Market demand** is the sum of all individual demands at a given price. At ₹50: $3 + 3 + 4 + 4 = 14$ kg. 3 kg is only your own demand, 3.5 kg is the average of the four buyers rather than their total, and 22 kg is the total for the ₹20 row, read from the wrong line.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
topic: Why the market demand curve is flatter
prompt: In the chapter's mango example, when the price falls from ₹150 to ₹50 per kg, Srivalli buys **2 kg more**, but market demand (Srivalli, Alex and Israt together) rises by **12 kg**. Why is the market demand curve **flatter** than Srivalli's demand curve?

image.alt: Two demand curves, P and Q, on the same price–quantity axes

options.text: Market demand adds up many buyers, so the same fall in price produces a much larger change in total quantity
Sellers charge lower prices in the market than they charge Srivalli on her own
The Law of Demand applies to the whole market but not to individual buyers
Market demand is the average of all buyers' demands, which smooths out the curve

hint: Compare 2 kg with 12 kg for the same change in price.
explanation: Market demand **aggregates** many consumers. For the same ₹100 fall in price, Srivalli's quantity rises by 2 kg (1 → 3 kg) but the market's rises by 12 kg (6 → 18 kg), so the market curve is **flatter and more responsive**. Everyone faces the same price, the Law of Demand applies to every buyer, and market demand is a **sum**, not an average.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: Srivalli buys 1 kg at ₹150 and 3 kg at ₹50, while the whole market buys 6 kg at ₹150 and 18 kg at ₹50. Tap the **market demand curve**.

image.alt: Two demand curves on price–quantity axes with numbered markers

spots.label: Curve P: Srivalli's individual demand curve

hint: Look for the curve that reaches 18 kg.
explanation: Curve Q passes through 6 kg at ₹150, 12 kg at ₹100 and 18 kg at ₹50, the totals for all three buyers, so it is the **market demand curve** (DmDm’ in the chapter). Curve P reaches only 3 kg: it is Srivalli's **individual demand curve**. Both slope downwards, but Q is flatter because it adds up many buyers.

A line on price–quantity axes
A line on price–quantity axes
A line on price–quantity axes

hint: As the price goes down, does the quantity go up or down?
explanation: Your schedule follows the **Law of Demand**: the lower the price, the more notebooks you buy, and at ₹60 you stop buying altogether. That inverse relationship gives a **downward-sloping** line (Graph R). An upward-sloping line is the shape of a supply curve, a flat line would mean the price never changes, and a vertical line would mean you buy the same number at every price.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: At a canteen, the price of coffee rises from ₹20 to ₹30 a cup, while tea stays at ₹15. What is most likely to happen to the **demand for tea**?

image.alt: A glass of tea and a mug of coffee with price tags

options.text: It falls, because all hot drinks become less popular
It stays exactly the same, because the price of tea has not changed
It falls, because tea and coffee are used together
It rises, because some coffee drinkers switch to tea

hint: Can tea and coffee replace each other?
explanation: Tea and coffee are **substitute goods**: they can replace each other. When a substitute (coffee) becomes dearer, people switch to the relatively cheaper option, so **demand for tea rises** even though its own price is unchanged. Goods that are used together are **complements**, which is not the case here.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A printer printing a page, next to an ink cartridge

assertion: If the demand for printers increases, the demand for printer cartridges may also rise, even if the price of cartridges does not change.
reason: Printers and cartridges are complementary goods, which are generally used together.
hint: Can you use one without the other?
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. **Complementary goods** are used together to give the consumer utility, so more printers in use means more cartridges are needed. The chapter's other examples are smartphones and earphones, cars and petrol, and movie tickets and cinema popcorn: if tickets get dearer, popcorn sales in the hall may fall.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: Select **all** the pairs that are **complementary goods** (goods used together).

image.alt: Four pairs of everyday goods shown side by side

options.text: Movie ticket and popcorn in the cinema hall

hint: Four are correct. Would you buy one instead of the other, or along with the other?
explanation: **Complements** are used together: a ticket with cinema popcorn, an eraser with a pencil, a notebook with a pen, and a mobile with earphones. **Substitutes** can replace each other: a laptop or a computer, an air conditioner or a cooler, an apple or a banana. A rise in the price of one substitute raises demand for the other, while a rise in the price of one complement lowers demand for the other.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: Suppose the price of petrol **doubles**. Select **all** the goods and services whose demand is likely to **rise**.

image.alt: A petrol pump whose price display is changing, with a car filling up

hint: Two of them let people travel without buying petrol.
explanation: Petrol and petrol cars are **complements**, so dearer petrol makes petrol cars, and the accessories that go with them, less attractive: their demand is likely to **fall**. Electric cars and public transport are **substitutes** for driving a petrol car, so their demand is likely to **rise**. Their own prices need not change at all for their demand to change.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: Match each determinant of demand with the example that shows it.

image.alt: Five round icons: a cup, a wallet, a heart, a snowflake and a calendar

right.text: Sweater shops are crowded once winter arrives
A family waits to buy a fridge, expecting festival discounts
Coffee gets dearer, so more people order tea
Srivalli keeps buying mangoes even though oranges are cheaper
After a salary rise, a family buys better-quality rice
A farmer plants chickpeas because their price is high

hint: One example is about a seller, not a buyer: it is left over.
explanation: Demand changes for reasons other than a good's own price: **related goods** (coffee and tea), **income** (more to spend, or higher quality), **taste and preference** (Srivalli will not swap mangoes for oranges), **seasonality** (weather, festivals and habits) and **future price expectations** (people postpone buying if they expect prices to fall). The farmer planting chickpeas is a **supply** decision.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: The make-up of a population shapes demand. In a town where **many elderly people** live, which kind of footwear would you expect to be in higher demand? Tap it.

image.alt: A shoe-shop shelf with four kinds of footwear and numbered markers

hint: Think about comfort and support for older feet.
explanation: Demand depends on the **size and composition** of the population. More children means more demand for **sports shoes**, more working adults for **formal shoes**, and more elderly people for **comfortable or orthopaedic shoes**. On size, the chapter notes that India, as the most populous nation, has large domestic consumer demand that contributes to its economic growth.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: The first mango tastes delicious, the second is good, but by the fourth you are barely interested. What does the chapter call this idea, and how does it affect demand?

image.alt: Four mangoes eaten one after another, with a bar and a face above each

options.text: Law of supply: sellers lower the price after each mango
Diminishing marginal utility: the extra satisfaction from each additional mango falls, so willingness to pay falls
Purchasing power: your money buys fewer mangoes each time
Seasonality: mangoes go out of season while you are eating them

hint: The key word is 'additional' satisfaction.
explanation: This is the **diminishing marginal utility** principle: the additional utility (usefulness or satisfaction) from a product falls as more of it is consumed. Because each extra mango is worth less to you, your **willingness to pay** for it falls, and so demand falls. In the example, the price, your money and the season have not changed.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: Demand for some goods depends on the time of year rather than on their price. Tap the shop that is likely to be crowded at the **start of a new academic session**.

image.alt: A street with four shops and numbered markers

hint: What do students need when school reopens?
explanation: This is **seasonality**: people demand different products at different times of the year, depending on weather, festivals and cultural habits. Bookshops fill up at the start of the academic session, sweet shops during the **festive season**, and sweaters and jackets sell in **winter**, even when prices have not changed.

topic: Law of supply and the supply curve
prompt: Seller A offers 1 kg of mangoes at ₹50, 2 kg at ₹100 and 3 kg at ₹150. Which graph shows this seller's **supply curve**?

image.alt: A line on price–quantity axes
A line on price–quantity axes
A line on price–quantity axes
A line on price–quantity axes

hint: Higher price, more offered for sale.
explanation: **Supply** is the quantity sellers are willing and able to offer at a particular price. By the **Law of Supply**, quantity supplied rises as price rises (a **direct** relationship), so the supply curve slopes **upwards** (Graph Q). Higher prices increase profitability, encourage producers to raise output and attract new firms. The downward-sloping line is a demand curve.

prompt: Three mango sellers, X, Y and Z, offer the quantities shown. What is the **market supply** at **₹80 per kg**?

image.alt: A table of how many kilograms of mangoes three sellers offer at three prices

hint: Add what every seller offers at the same price.
explanation: **Market supply** is the sum of all individual supplies at a price: at ₹80, $4 + 5 + 7 = 16$ kg. 4 kg is Seller X alone, 7 kg is only the largest single seller, and 24 kg is the total for ₹120 (6 + 8 + 10), read from the wrong row. Market supply rises with price here (6, 16, 24 kg), as the law of supply predicts.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: Two mango trees with a few mangoes slowly ripening

assertion: At the start of the mango season, mangoes are cheap because plenty of them reach the market.
reason: In the middle of the season, the supply of mangoes increases and their price falls.
hint: How many mangoes are ripe in the first few weeks?
explanation: The assertion is false: at the start of the season **supply is low**, which makes mangoes **costly**. The reason is true: mid-season, supply rises and prices fall. The general rule in the chapter is that when supply is less than demand, prices rise, and when supply exceeds demand, prices fall.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: Match each determinant of supply with its example.

image.alt: Four round icons: two crops, three stalls, a refrigerated truck and a storehouse

right.text: Cold-storage trucks let mangoes reach distant markets
Potato wholesalers hold back stock, expecting higher prices in the peak season
Chickpea prices are high, so a farmer grows chickpeas instead of wheat next season
Many new juice stalls open on one street, and juice becomes cheaper
Bookshops get crowded when the school year begins

hint: One example is about buyers' demand and is left over.
explanation: A farmer compares the **profitability of alternatives**, so a high chickpea price draws land away from wheat. **More sellers** push market supply above demand, so prices fall. Better **technology** (drip irrigation, weather sensors, cold storage) lowers costs and raises supply. If sellers **expect** higher prices later, they may hold back supply now. Crowded bookshops show seasonal **demand**.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: A farmer switches from watering his field by hand to **drip irrigation**, which cuts water use by **40%** and raises yield by **30%**. He used to harvest **40 quintals** of tomatoes. How much does he harvest now?

image.alt: Tomato plants watered drop by drop from a pipe along the field

hint: Find 30% of 40 and add it on. The 40% is about water, not yield.
explanation: Increase $= \dfrac{30}{100} \times 40 = 12$ quintals, so the new harvest is $40 + 12 = 52$ quintals. 70 adds 30 quintals instead of 30%, 56 wrongly uses the 40% water figure, and 28 takes 30% away instead of adding it. Lower water and labour costs plus a higher yield mean he is **willing to supply more at every price**.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
topic: Effect of better technology on the market
prompt: Suppose **many** farmers in a region adopt drip irrigation. What is the most likely effect on the tomato market, other things remaining the same?

image.alt: A demand curve with a supply curve sliding sideways and the crossing point moving

options.text: Demand for tomatoes rises, so their price rises
Supply falls, because farmers now use less water
Market supply rises at every price, so the equilibrium price tends to fall and more is sold
Nothing changes, because the price of tomatoes has not changed

hint: Technology lowers the cost of producing each kilogram.
explanation: Better **technology** reduces the cost of production, so producers supply more at each price and the supply curve moves to the right, as in the animation. With demand unchanged, the new crossing point has a **lower price** and a **larger quantity**. Buyers' demand has not changed, and using less water is a cost saving, not a cut in output.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: The table shows the tomato market one morning. What are the **equilibrium price** and **equilibrium quantity**?

image.alt: A table of quantities of tomatoes demanded and supplied at five prices

hint: Find the row where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
explanation: **Market equilibrium** is where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied: at ₹40 both are 30 kg, so the market is **cleared**, with neither a shortage nor a surplus. ₹20 is where demand is largest and ₹60 where supply is largest, but at both prices the two quantities differ. 60 kg wrongly adds demand and supply together.

subject: social
chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: In the same tomato market, suppose the price is stuck at **₹30 per kg**. What does the market face?

image.alt: A table of quantities of tomatoes demanded and supplied at five prices

hint: Compare quantity demanded with quantity supplied at ₹30.
explanation: At ₹30, buyers want 40 kg but only 20 kg is supplied: $40 - 20 = 20$ kg of **excess demand**, a **shortage**. Calling it a surplus gets the direction wrong, since supply is the smaller number. 60 kg adds the two quantities, and 10 kg compares supply with the equilibrium quantity (30 − 20) instead of with demand. Below the equilibrium price there is always a shortage.

subject: social
chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: Now suppose the tomato price is **₹60 per kg**. What happens in the market?

image.alt: A table of quantities of tomatoes demanded and supplied at five prices

hint: At ₹60, which is bigger: quantity supplied or quantity demanded?
explanation: At ₹60, sellers offer 50 kg but buyers want only 10 kg: $50 - 10 = 40$ kg of **excess supply**, a **surplus**. It is not a shortage, because supply exceeds demand. 20 kg compares supply with the equilibrium quantity (50 − 30), and 60 kg adds the two figures. Above the equilibrium price, unsold stock piles up and pushes the price down.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: Demand curve DD’ and supply curve SS’ are drawn for a market. Tap the point that shows **market equilibrium**.

image.alt: Demand and supply curves with two dashed price lines and numbered markers

hint: It is where the two curves cross.
explanation: **Equilibrium** is where the demand curve intersects the supply curve: here at **₹200 per kg and 30 kg**. At that price quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so there is no pressure for the price to change and the market is cleared. Every other marked point lies on only one curve, at a price where the two quantities differ.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
topic: Surplus and shortage on a graph
prompt: The upper and lower dashed lines show two prices that are not the equilibrium price. Tap the gap that shows a **surplus (excess supply)**.

image.alt: Demand and supply curves with two dashed price lines and numbered markers

spots.label: Equilibrium price on the price axis

hint: Above the equilibrium price, sellers want to sell more than buyers want to buy.
explanation: At ₹300 (upper line), buyers want only 10 kg (the point on DD’) but sellers offer 50 kg (the point on SS’), so the gap is a **surplus of 40 kg**. At ₹100 (lower line) it is the reverse: buyers want 50 kg but only 10 kg is supplied, a **shortage**. In a free market a surplus pushes the price down and a shortage pushes it up, towards ₹200.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
topic: How a shortage moves the market to equilibrium
prompt: The price of mangoes is **below** the equilibrium price. Put in order what happens next in a free market.

image.alt: A long queue of buyers in front of a mango stall with only a few mangoes

items.text: Buyers are willing to pay more, and sellers raise the price
The gap closes where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied
Quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied at this low price
As the price rises, quantity demanded falls and quantity supplied rises
A shortage appears: queues form and some buyers go home empty-handed

hint: Start with the cause (the low price) and end with equilibrium.
explanation: Below equilibrium there is **excess demand** (Qs < Qd), so the market faces a **shortage**. When supply is less than demand, **prices rise**. A higher price makes buyers want less and sellers offer more, until the market reaches **equilibrium** and is cleared. A surplus works the other way and pushes the price down.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
topic: Does equilibrium exist in the real world?
prompt: Read the Assertion (A) and Reason (R) carefully.

image.alt: A balance with D on one pan and S on the other, tipping back and forth

assertion: In real-world markets, the equilibrium keeps moving and never fully settles.
reason: At equilibrium, the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied.
hint: Both statements are correct. Does the definition of equilibrium explain why it keeps shifting?
explanation: Both are true, but R does not explain A: R only **defines** equilibrium. A is true because changes in **technology, wages, interest rates, wars, political events, pandemics, weather and natural disasters** keep shifting demand and supply, so the market is always adjusting to a new equilibrium. Those changing conditions are what explain A.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: Arrange the story of face-mask prices during the COVID-19 pandemic of 2020, as told in the chapter.

image.alt: A line graph of the price of face masks over time, with a mask drawn beside it

items.text: Suppliers adjust to the higher demand and prices fall
The pandemic begins and demand for face masks surges
The pandemic ends, demand drops further and prices return to pre-pandemic levels
Supply cannot catch up immediately, so mask prices rise sharply

hint: Demand moved first; supply took time to respond.
explanation: Demand for masks **surged** in 2020 and supply could not keep up, so prices **rose significantly**. Over time suppliers **adjusted** and prices fell. Once the pandemic was over, demand fell further and prices returned to **pre-pandemic levels**. The example shows a real market always moving towards a new equilibrium.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: During the festive season, people buy more sweets at every price. The demand curve shifts from **D1** to **D2**, while supply **S** does not change. Tap the **new equilibrium**.

image.alt: A supply curve with two demand curves and numbered markers

spots.label: On new demand D2 at the old price ₹200

hint: The new equilibrium is where the NEW demand curve meets the supply curve.
explanation: Equilibrium is always where demand meets supply. After the shift, **D2 meets S at ₹250 and 40 kg**, so higher demand raises both the equilibrium price and quantity. The point on D2 at the old price of ₹200 shows that if the price stayed at ₹200, buyers would want 50 kg while sellers offer only 30 kg, a shortage that pushes the price up.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: One of the chapter's Big Questions: the same flight seat costs **₹3,000** on one day and **₹9,000** on another. By what **percentage** is the higher fare above the lower one?

image.alt: An aeroplane flying across the sky with two ticket price tags below

hint: % change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100.
explanation: $\%\ \text{change} = \dfrac{9000 - 3000}{3000} \times 100 = \dfrac{6000}{3000} \times 100 = 200\%$. 300% is the new fare as a percentage of the old one (three times as much), not the increase. 66.7% divides the rise by the new fare instead of the old, and 33.3% is the old fare as a share of the new. Fares change like this because demand differs from day to day.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: A hotel in Goa charges **₹8,000** a night for a Saturday in December. A group tour cancels, so the hotel **cuts the tariff by 40%** overnight to fill the empty rooms. What is the new tariff?

image.alt: A seaside hotel with room-rate tags for different days

hint: Find 40% of ₹8,000, then take it away.
explanation: Cut $= \dfrac{40}{100} \times 8000 = 3200$, so the new tariff is ₹8,000 − ₹3,200 = **₹4,800**. ₹3,200 is only the size of the cut, ₹7,960 subtracts ₹40 instead of 40%, and ₹11,200 adds the cut. Hotels change tariffs like this, sometimes several times a day, to earn maximum **revenue**: the total money earned from sales before expenses.

image.alt: Four calendar pages for different nights at a hotel, each with an unknown room rate

items.text: A Saturday in December (tourist season)
A Monday in July (off-season)
New Year's Eve
A December Saturday after a group tour cancels and the tariff is cut by 40%

explanation: The tariffs are ₹1,500 (Monday in July, off-season), ₹4,800 (the December Saturday after a 40% cut on ₹8,000), ₹8,000 (Saturday in December) and ₹25,000 (**New Year's Eve**, very high demand). The same room costs different amounts because **demand** changes with the season, events and how fast rooms are booked, which makes the market **dynamic**.

The number of floors in the hotel building
A single fixed rate set for the whole year

assertion: Overfishing to meet today's high demand can reduce the supply of fish in the future.
reason: When a resource is used up faster than it can recover, less of it is left for the future.
hint: Fish need time to breed and grow back.
explanation: Both are true and R explains A. The chapter's Think About It box warns that high demand for fast fashion, **overfishing** and the overuse of **groundwater** can harm **future supply**. Chasing only short-term gains leaves less to sell later and pushes prices up, so long-term **sustainability** also affects market equilibrium.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: A **price floor** (a legal minimum price) has an effect only if it is set **above** the equilibrium price. Tap the line that would be an **effective price floor** in this market.

image.alt: Demand and supply curves with two green dashed price lines and numbered markers

hint: A minimum price below ₹200 would not stop anyone from trading at ₹200.
explanation: Equilibrium here is ₹200. A minimum price of **₹300** holds the price above equilibrium, so it really changes the market (and leaves excess supply). A minimum of ₹100 would have no effect, because the market price of ₹200 is already higher. A **minimum wage** is a price floor; a **price ceiling** is a maximum price, such as one set for essential medicines.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
topic: Price ceiling below the market price
prompt: Suppose the government sets a **maximum** sale price for an essential vaccine that is **below** the market-driven price, like the ₹100 line on this graph where equilibrium is ₹200. What is most likely to happen?

image.alt: Demand and supply curves with two green dashed price lines across the graph

options.text: A fall in the demand for vaccines

hint: At the lower price, compare how much buyers want with how much sellers offer.
explanation: A price ceiling below equilibrium makes quantity demanded **greater** than quantity supplied: on this graph, at ₹100 buyers want 50 units but sellers offer only 10, so there is a **shortage**. Producers receive less and may lose the motivation to supply. A surplus needs a price above equilibrium, and a lower price raises, not lowers, the quantity demanded.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
prompt: The market price of wheat is **₹30 per kg**, but the government sets a **maximum price of ₹20 per kg**. A farmer sells **800 kg**. How much **less** does he earn than he would in a free market?

image.alt: Sacks of wheat beside a farmer, with a market price tag and a maximum price tag

hint: Find the loss on each kilogram, then multiply by the quantity.
explanation: Loss per kg = ₹30 − ₹20 = ₹10, so the total loss = ₹10 × 800 = **₹8,000**. ₹16,000 is what he earns at the capped price (₹20 × 800) and ₹24,000 is what he would earn in a free market (₹30 × 800). ₹10 is the loss on just one kilogram. Lower earnings like this can **reduce production and cause shortages**, one limitation of government intervention.

prompt: Match each term with its meaning.

right.text: Illegal trade in goods or services that are banned or regulated
The highest price a seller is allowed to charge
Storing goods beyond present need, expecting shortages or higher prices
A single seller controlling the whole supply of a product with no close substitutes

hint: A ceiling is above you; a floor is below you. One meaning is left over.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
topic: Why public goods need the government
prompt: A neighbourhood park will cost **₹4,00,000**. The plan is for each family to give **₹5,000**, but only **50 families** pay, because the others think, 'If others pay, I can use it for free.' How much money is **still missing**?

image.alt: A row of houses and a collection box for building a neighbourhood park

hint: First find how much the 50 families give.
explanation: Collected = 50 × ₹5,000 = ₹2,50,000, so the shortfall is ₹4,00,000 − ₹2,50,000 = **₹1,50,000** (the share of the 30 families who did not pay). ₹2,50,000 is the amount collected, not the gap; ₹6,50,000 adds the two; and ₹15,000 drops a zero. This 'others will pay' thinking is why goods that benefit everyone often need **government provision or funding**.

topic: Why the government steps into markets
prompt: India is a market-based, regulated economy. Select **all** the actions or reasons for government intervention that the chapter describes.

image.alt: Five round icons about prices, sellers and goods kept in storage

options.text: Keeping essentials like medicines affordable, especially for low-income groups
Providing public goods such as roads and streetlights
Setting the price of every good sold in the country
Stopping monopolies from charging high prices and restricting supply
Guaranteeing that every business makes a profit
Levying higher taxes on tobacco and alcohol to promote healthier choices

hint: Four are correct. Markets still decide most prices.
explanation: Markets allocate goods by **willingness and ability to pay**, which can leave essentials out of reach, so the government ensures **fairness and equity** (through price ceilings and minimum wages), provides **public goods**, checks **monopolies**, and taxes harmful products such as tobacco. India, the world's fourth-largest economy, still lets demand and supply set most prices: the government neither fixes every price nor promises profits.

chapter: The Price Puzzle: What Drives the Market
topic: Why prices change during the day
prompt: At a vegetable market, tomatoes sell for ₹40 per kg in the morning but only ₹20 per kg by evening. Which explanation uses **demand and supply** best?

image.alt: A tomato seller's stall in the morning and in the evening, with price tags

options.text: Sellers have unsold tomatoes that will spoil and fewer buyers are left, so supply exceeds demand
The government orders every seller to halve vegetable prices after sunset each day
Evening shoppers have more money to spend, so sellers can accept a lower price from them
Tomatoes sold in the morning cost farmers more to grow than those sold in the evening

hint: Tomatoes spoil quickly. What does a seller want to avoid at closing time?
explanation: This is one of the chapter's Big Questions and a market-visit activity. Fresh tomatoes cannot be stored for long, so by evening sellers want to clear their stock before it spoils, while many buyers have already shopped. When **supply exceeds demand**, prices fall. No government order is involved, and richer buyers would not make sellers lower their prices.
